title: PSTN choices
blurb: Cisco Calling Plan, Cloud Connected PSTN, and premises PSTN through a local gateway. Cloud PSTN does not serve premises-originated calls.

lessons.title: The three PSTN models
lessons.summary: Every location picks one connection. Cisco Calling Plan and Cloud Connected PSTN are cloud PSTN. Premises PSTN keeps your carrier or your PBX behind a local gateway.
objectives: Keep one trunk on a premises location

diagram.caption: One location, one PSTN connection type.

steps.detail: The connection is per location.

steps.label: Cloud
steps.detail: Both are cloud PSTN. Cisco's article says cloud PSTN serves Webex Calling users.

steps.label: Select a trunk
steps.detail: Create the trunk first. Only one trunk for that location.
steps.inspect: Same trunk may be reused elsewhere

steps.label: Blocked
steps.detail: Calls that originate from premises users cannot access cloud PSTN.

paragraphs: Cisco PSTN is the Calling Plan: emergency, inbound, outbound, and number order or port where it is offered. CCP is the partner cloud option.
Premises PSTN is how you keep a provider or connect a non-cloud site. The local gateway becomes the trunk.

cite.label: Trunks, route groups, and dial plans

paragraphs: The trunk article says cloud PSTN, whether Cisco PSTN or CCP, can only provide PSTN access for Webex Calling users. Calls originating from premises users cannot access cloud PSTN.
A factory PBX does not borrow the headquarters Calling Plan for its outbound calls. Give that PBX its own trunks.

fault.symptom: A Unified CM user's national calls fail after someone removes the PRI and points the route pattern at Webex Calling cloud PSTN.

fault.title: Double PSTN
fault.symptom: A location is set to CCP and someone also sends its DID range out a local PRI, so inbound calls split.
fault.log: SYNTHETIC: DID 2125550100 on CCP and on the PRI.
fault.cause: One location has one connection type. A number should have one owner.
fault.fix: Choose the owner, remove the duplicate route, and place one inbound test.

paragraphs: Unmatched Webex Calling destinations go to the local gateway. That is the default premises fallthrough in the workflow guide.

lessons.title: Choosing in a design review
lessons.summary: Pick PSTN from facts: who owns the numbers, where the users register, and whether the call originates on premises. Everything else is taste.

steps.inspect: Port is a project, not a checkbox

steps.label: Where do they register?
steps.detail: Webex Calling, Dedicated Instance, or the PBX you still run.

steps.label: Who places the outbound call?

steps.label: One connection

sections.h: Mixed designs are normal. Mixed rules are not.
paragraphs: A company can use Calling Plan at HQ and a local gateway at a factory. Each location has its own connection.
What you cannot do is let the factory's PBX users consume the HQ Calling Plan. That is the origin rule, not a style preference.

lessons.title: PSTN fault patterns
lessons.summary: Most PSTN incidents are an origin rule, a missing pattern, a second trunk, or an emergency path that nobody tested. The signaling ports come next, with the gateway.
objectives: Avoid changing certificates when the dial plan is the fault

diagram.caption: Four fault shapes you can recognize from a trace.

steps.label: Who called?
steps.detail: Premises PBX versus Webex user. The block only applies to the premises origin on cloud PSTN.

steps.label: Did a pattern match?
steps.detail: If not, premises fallthrough uses the location trunk. Cloud uses cloud PSTN.

steps.label: How many selected?
steps.detail: Two is already a fault on a premises location.

steps.label: If the call was emergency
steps.detail: Do not debug a dial plan pattern for 911 until you know whether the location is enabled for RedSky or Intrado.

paragraphs: Origin, then pattern, then trunk count, then emergency. Certificate errors look like timeouts and 403s, which you will meet on the gateway track.
A 403 with a name mismatch is not a dial-plan miss. Read the SIP response before you edit patterns.

cite.label: RFC 3261, SIP

Was the caller a Webex user dialing a teammate? Then location prefixes are in scope. Different articles.
